newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends flat ahead of key US employment report.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends flat ahead of key US employment report.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed in U.S. trading on Thursday, adhering to extremely tight ranges against the mark and yen ahead of key U.S. employment data, due Friday.

"The dollar has really been confined to very narrow trading ranges in anticipation of the employment numbers on Friday," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.
"But I think the dollar remains well underpinned because of the turmoil going on in Europe," he added.
The release of new seasonal adjustment factors by the Bureau of Labor Statistics last week led some forecasters to revise down their estimates for payrolls.
But many in the market are still expecting a robust report, which traders said could push the dollar to fresh peaks against the mark.

"If it comes in near consensus it would confirm nice job creation in stark contrast to what's going on in Germany and could give us enough of a push to challenge, if not Friday then next week, the highs of the year against the mark," said Bob Near, vice president at Bank of New York.

According to the latest Reuters poll, Wall Street economists are forecasting a rise of 219,000 in May non-farm jobs. The unemployment rate is expected to tick up to 5.0 percent from a 23-year low of 4.9 percent last month, and average hourly earnings are seen rising 0.4 percent in May.

In Germany on Thursday, official sources confirmed to Reuters newspaper leaks of an unadjusted drop of roughly 90,000 in May unemployment -- far less than many economists were expecting in a month where strong economic activity traditionally boosts the jobs market.

Little moved, but well-supported according to traders, the dollar ended at 1.7275/80 marks on Thursday against 1.7285/95 at the open. Against the yen, the dollar was also little changed at 115.60/70 versus 115.62/72 at the outset of trading.

Lingering concerns over European monetary union prospects, in the wake of Sunday's French elections and a week-long gold revaluation row between the German government and Bundesbank, played second fiddle to the payrolls vigil on Thursday.
But dealers said Europe's troubles were far from over and predicted ongoing pressure on European currencies.

"I think the dollar will continue to trade higher against Europe, but against the yen it is the exact opposite," said Nelson of ABN-AMRO. "So you're probably going to see the yen stronger against Europe."

In overseas trading on Thursday, the dollar weakened below the 116 yen threshold after Yasuo Matsushita, Governor of the Bank of Japan, told a parliamentary committee that it was important to take preemptive policy steps in order to realize continued growth without inflation.

Elsewhere, sterling pushed to a higher close of $1.6340/50 against $1.6285/90 at the open. The Bank of England's new policy-setting council will meet on Friday and some market participants are expecting another quarter-point rise in interest rates.
The dollar ended at 1.4462/72 Swiss francs, up from 1.4440/50 at the open.
It ended little changed at Canadian $1.3765/70 against C$1.3763/68, while the Australian dollar ended at $0.7611/16, just up from $0.7601/06.
